title: Adult cardiac arrest (ALS/ACLS)
subject: emergency
summary: High-quality CPR with minimal interruptions, early defibrillation for VF/pVT, adrenaline 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes (as soon as possible for non-shockable rhythms, after failed initial shocks for shockable rhythms), amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VF/pVT, and an active search for reversible causes.

sections.title: Recognise and call for help
items: Unresponsive with absent or abnormal (agonal) breathing: treat as cardiac arrest. Take no more than 10 seconds to feel for a central pulse; if in doubt, start CPR.
Call the resuscitation team (code blue), bring a defibrillator and note the time of collapse.
Many in-hospital arrests have warning signs: use a track-and-trigger score (for example NEWS2) and act on deterioration early.

sections.title: High-quality CPR and defibrillation
items: Compress the centre of the chest at 100 to 120/min, depth at least 5 cm (not more than 6 cm), allow full recoil; change the compressor every 2 minutes or sooner if tired.
No advanced airway: 30:2 with bag-mask and 100% oxygen. With a tracheal tube or supraglottic airway: 10 breaths/min (1 every 6 seconds) with continuous compressions. Avoid hyperventilation.

Antero-lateral pads (lateral pad directly below the armpit in the mid-axillary line). Keep compressing while charging, keep the pre-shock pause under 5 seconds and resume compressions straight after the shock without a pulse check.
Energy: biphasic per manufacturer (AHA: usually 120 to 200 J; ERC: first shock at least 150 J), same or higher for later shocks; use the maximum if the setting is unknown. Monophasic 360 J.
Rhythm check every 2 minutes. Check a pulse only if an organised rhythm appears or there are signs of ROSC (sudden ETCO2 rise, arterial waveform, purposeful movement).
Witnessed, monitored VF/pVT with a defibrillator already attached (cath lab, CCU): up to 3 stacked shocks may be given; count them as the first shock for drug timing.

sections.title: Drugs, access and airway
items: Access: attempt IV first; use IO if IV fails after 2 attempts or is not feasible. The tracheal route is no longer recommended for drugs.
Non-shockable rhythm (asystole, PEA): adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as possible, then every 3 to 5 minutes.

Shockable rhythm (VF/pVT): adrenaline 1 mg after initial shocks fail (ERC: after the 3rd shock), then every 3 to 5 minutes. Amiodarone 300 mg after 3 shocks and a further 150 mg after 5 shocks; lidocaine is an alternative.

Refractory VF (persisting after 3 shocks): recheck pad position and consider a vector change to antero-posterior pads. AHA 2025 says double sequential defibrillation may be considered; RCUK does not recommend it routinely.
Airway: start with bag-mask; progress to a supraglottic airway or tracheal tube only if skilled (compression pause under 5 seconds). Confirm tube position with a sustained waveform capnography trace.
Do not give calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium or steroids routinely; reserve them for specific causes (hyperkalaemia, sodium channel blocker toxicity, torsades de pointes).

sections.title: Reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts)
items: Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic causes (including hypoglycaemia and acidosis), hypothermia; thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins.
Hyperkalaemic arrest: 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride IV and 50 mmol sodium bicarbonate IV (separate lines or flush between), then insulin-glucose; consider dialysis or ECPR if CPR fails.
Suspected or confirmed pulmonary embolism: give thrombolysis and continue CPR for 60 to 90 minutes afterwards.
Point-of-care ultrasound can show tamponade, pneumothorax or hypovolaemia but must not lengthen pauses; right ventricular dilatation alone does not diagnose PE.
India: think of poisoning (organophosphates, aluminium phosphide, yellow oleander), snakebite, hyperkalaemia in CKD and electrolyte loss from diarrhoeal illness.

sections.title: Monitoring during CPR
items: Waveform capnography: ETCO2 below 10 mmHg suggests poor CPR quality or poor prognosis; above 10 and ideally above 20 mmHg is associated with ROSC. An abrupt sustained rise suggests ROSC.

With an arterial line (physiology-guided CPR, ERC): aim for diastolic pressure 30 mmHg or more and ETCO2 25 mmHg (3.3 kPa) or more. In highly monitored arrests, adrenaline may be given in 50 to 100 microgram increments first.
Record times of shocks and drugs aloud; use a timer and CPR feedback device if available.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Pregnancy (fundus at or above the umbilicus): continuous manual left uterine displacement, IV access above the diaphragm, stop IV magnesium and give calcium if on magnesium, and prepare resuscitative delivery aiming for 5 minutes if no ROSC.
Hypothermia, drowning and anaphylaxis: follow the specific protocols (modified shock and drug rules below 30 degrees C; 5 initial rescue breaths in drowning).
CPR-induced consciousness: small doses of sedative or analgesic (for example fentanyl, ketamine, midazolam) may be used; never give a neuromuscular blocker alone to a conscious patient.

sections.title: Escalation and stopping
items: ECPR (VA-ECMO) may be considered for selected refractory arrests (witnessed, short no-flow time, likely reversible cause) where a system exists; decide early.
Use mechanical compression devices only when high-quality manual CPR is impractical or unsafe (transport, cath lab, prolonged CPR).
Stopping is a team decision based on cause, duration, rhythm, comorbidity and known wishes. ETCO2 of 10 mmHg or less after 20 minutes of ALS may be one part of that decision, never the only basis.
Check for a valid DNACPR decision and follow institutional policy.

sections.title: After ROSC
items: Move to post-cardiac arrest care: ABCDE, 12-lead ECG, SpO2 90 to 98% (ERC 94 to 98%), PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, MAP 65 mmHg or more, and a temperature control strategy.
Emergency coronary angiography for persistent ST elevation or suspected ongoing coronary occlusion; admit to ICU.
Debrief the team and document the event.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Long pauses for pulse checks, intubation or ultrasound; leaning on the chest; compressor fatigue.
Missed oesophageal intubation: a flat capnography trace means the tube is in the oesophagus until proven otherwise.
Delaying the first shock in VF to give drugs, place an airway or obtain IV access.
Treating PEA without actively looking for hypovolaemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE and hyperkalaemia.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
drugs.dose: 1 mg IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes (1 mL of 1 mg/mL or 10 mL of 0.1 mg/mL), followed by a 20 mL saline flush
drugs.notes: Non-shockable: as soon as possible. Shockable: after initial shocks fail (ERC: after the 3rd shock).

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.dose: 300 mg IV or IO bolus after the 3rd shock; further 150 mg after the 5th shock
drugs.notes: Refractory or recurrent VF/pVT. May be diluted to 20 mL with 5% glucose.

drugs.name: Lidocaine (lignocaine)
drugs.dose: AHA: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg IV or IO, then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg. ERC: 100 mg IV, further 50 mg after the 5th shock
drugs.notes: Alternative when amiodarone is unavailable or by local policy.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.notes: Hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, calcium channel blocker or magnesium toxicity only. Not routine.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4%
drugs.notes: Hyperkalaemic arrest, tricyclic or other sodium channel blocker toxicity. Not routine.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: Torsades de pointes or suspected hypomagnesaemia.
